stem: A worker's monthly wages and price index (base 2020 = 100) are shown below. 2020: Rs 20,000, index 100. 2021: Rs 22,000, index 110. 2022: Rs 25,000, index 120. 2023: Rs 28,000, index 140. In which year was the real wage highest?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Student does not deflate and picks the base year. Real wage in 2020 = 20,000 / 100 × 100 = Rs 20,000, which is not the highest.
Student notes the nominal wage rose but does not deflate. Real wage in 2021 = 22,000 / 110 × 100 = Rs 20,000, same as 2020.
Student picks the year with the highest nominal wage (Rs 28,000) without deflating. Real wage in 2023 = 28,000 / 140 × 100 = Rs 20,000.

explanation: Deflate each year: Real = (Nominal / Index) × 100. 2020: 20,000. 2021: 22,000/110×100 = 20,000. 2022: 25,000/120×100 = 20,833. 2023: 28,000/140×100 = 20,000. The real wage peaked in 2022, though the nominal wage kept rising.

explanation_sections.punchline: Only 2022 gives a deflated real wage above Rs 20,000. Every other year deflates back to exactly Rs 20,000.
explanation_sections.approach: Deflating problems require one calculation per row: Real wage = (Nominal wage / Price index) × 100. Build a small column of real wages before comparing. Never compare nominal wages directly when prices have changed across years.
explanation_sections.lesson: A rising nominal wage does not mean a rising real wage. Always deflate before comparing purchasing power across time periods.
explanation_sections.timing: About 120 seconds. Four divisions with simple numbers. Eliminate 2023 in 10 seconds by noting the index rose proportionally with wages. Work 2022 last if time is short.
